The jug is an aerophone that uses an empty jar or bottle as resonator, classified Hornbostel–Sachs 421.13, and found mainly in North American and American music. The player uses a brass-like embouchure, holds the mouth of the jug about an inch from the lips, and blows a stream of air with vibrating lips; the jug never touches the mouth and acts only as a resonating chamber, and pitch is controlled by the tightness of the lips. Its range reaches two octaves, its timbre is low and hoarse, and it usually takes the bass and rhythm part beneath higher instruments such as the fiddle and harmonica, while also often soloing. It is mostly used in jug bands, and appears in a variant in early Cuban music.
演奏吹壺時，以類似銅管的口型，將壺口約距嘴一吋，不接觸嘴唇，再以唇震發聲吹入壺中: In playing the jug the player uses a brass-like embouchure, holding the mouth about an inch from the lips without touching them, and sounds it by blowing a lip buzz into the jug; the jug acts as a resonator, amplifying and rounding the lip tone. Pitch is controlled mainly by relaxing or tightening the lips, and a skilled player reaches two octaves. A beginner can first steady the distance and the lip buzz, then try adding voice, didgeridoo-style vocalisation or circular breathing. In performance, standing with the back to a wall reflects the sound towards the audience.
陶罐作為樂器時，常見器身以玻璃或炻器製成，最常見為陶瓷罐；亦有玻璃罐與瓶、塑膠漂: When a jar is used as an instrument, the body is commonly glass or stoneware, most often a ceramic jar; glass jars and bottles, plastic bleach bottles and tin kerosene cans are also used. There is also a stovepipe, usually a piece of tin pipe three or four inches in diameter, about seventy-five or a hundred millimetres. The sounding body is the player's lips and the vessel acts only as a resonator; the source does not state the materials of other parts.
陶罐作為樂器的流行高峰見於1920年代，陶罐樂團活躍；因便宜、易攜帶而流行。除陶: The popularity of the jug as an instrument peaked in the 1920s, when jug bands were active; it was popular because it was cheap and easy to carry. Besides ceramic jugs, glass jars, plastic bleach bottles and tin kerosene cans were used, and material and size affect the timbre. It is mainly an acoustic instrument, but amplified or electric versions occasionally exist, and it appears on recordings by 1960s psychedelic bands. In the early Cuban music form son there is a version called the botija; well-known modern players include Fritz Richmond and Josh Smith.
陶罐屬氣鳴樂器，發聲分類為421.13。演奏者以類似銅管樂器的口風，將嘴唇震動直: The jug is an aerophone, classified 421.13 for sound production. The player uses a brass-like embouchure and blows the lip vibration directly into the mouth of the jug, held about an inch from the mouth, without the vessel touching the lips; it acts only as a resonator, amplifying and enriching the lip tone. Its timbre is low and hoarse, with something of the trombone's quality, and it usually lies below instruments such as the fiddle and harmonica. Pitch is controlled by the tightness of the lips, and a skilled player reaches two octaves. Compared with sounding a bottle directly across its mouth, which is quieter, usually gives a single pitch and belongs to bottle blowing, the jug enters the band by lip vibration, taking the bass and rhythm part, and can solo.
